title: World Models & Predictive Learning
blurb: Tests the three families of world model, why JEPA predicts embeddings instead of pixels, its three parts, why the EMA target encoder prevents representation collapse, how other methods prevent it, explicit dynamics models, and how to check a model learned something real.

refLinks.label: §60.2.1 Latent-Space Predictive Models: the JEPA Family

ideas.title: Representation collapse and the EMA target

refLinks.label: §60.2.2 Why the EMA Target Encoder Isn’t Optional

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter say pixel-space world models waste effort?
options: Pixel models can only predict one frame ahead.
Pixels can't be used as input to neural networks at all.
Most pixels are irrelevant detail, wasting capacity.
Pixel models need labels for every frame of video.
questions.explanation: Predicting every pixel spends capacity on texture and noise that don't matter for planning. Latent predictors predict embeddings instead.

questions.prompt: What does a pixel-space model give you that a latent model doesn't, without extra work?
options: Lower compute cost per prediction
Better sample efficiency on downstream tasks
Protection against representation collapse
A predicted frame you can look at directly
questions.explanation: Latent embeddings are opaque without a decoder or probe. Pixel models pay for their viewable output with far more compute.

questions.prompt: What does JEPA predict for a masked region?
options: Its embedding from the target encoder
The next action a robot should take
A class label for the object in it
Its raw pixel values, one by one
questions.explanation: Predicting embeddings lets the model drop irrelevant texture and lighting while keeping structure.

refLinks.label: §60.2.1 Latent-Space Predictive Models: the JEPA Family

questions.prompt: In JEPA, which network receives gradients directly?
options: The target encoder only
All three networks equally
None. JEPA trains without gradients.
The context encoder and predictor
questions.explanation: The target encoder is an EMA of the context encoder with no gradient of its own. The predictor and context encoder are trained.

refLinks.label: §60.2.1 Latent-Space Predictive Models: the JEPA Family

questions.prompt: mask_indices in Listing 60.1 is called with n_patches = 16, mask_ratio = 0.75 and min_context = 1. How many context patches stay visible?
questions.explanation: n_mask = min(int(16 × 0.75), 16 − 1) = min(12, 15) = 12. That leaves 16 − 12 = 4 context patches.

questions.prompt: What goes wrong if the masking ratio is too low?
options: The predictor can just copy neighbours.
Training runs out of memory.
The predictor has no context left to condition on.
The EMA update stops working.
questions.explanation: Too little masking makes prediction easy and teaches little. Too much leaves no useful context. Both weaken what the encoder learns.

options: The model forgets its earlier training after a few epochs.
All inputs map to nearly one embedding, so loss looks great.
The embeddings grow without bound until training diverges.
The predictor stops receiving gradients from the loss.
questions.explanation: If the target can move freely, collapsing everything to one point makes the loss near zero while learning nothing.

refLinks.label: §60.2.2 Why the EMA Target Encoder Isn’t Optional

questions.prompt: An EMA update uses momentum 0.99. A target weight is 1.0 and the online weight is 2.0. What is the target weight after one update?
questions.explanation: target = 0.99 × 1.0 + 0.01 × 2.0 = 1.01. The target moves slowly toward the online network.

questions.prompt: How does VICReg prevent collapse without a separate target encoder?
options: A term that penalises low variance across the batch
A slowly updated EMA copy of the encoder
Labels for a small subset of the training images
Stop-gradient on one branch plus an asymmetric predictor
questions.explanation: VICReg makes collapse costly rather than architecturally impossible. Stop-gradient with asymmetry is SimSiam, and the EMA target is JEPA and BYOL.

refLinks.label: §60.2.2 Why the EMA Target Encoder Isn’t Optional

questions.prompt: What happens if EMA momentum is set too low?
options: The masking ratio effectively doubles.
The target follows too closely.
The target barely moves, so learning slows down.
The predictor stops being trained.
questions.explanation: Low momentum means fast target updates, close to lockstep. Too high and the target goes stale, slowing learning.

questions.prompt: How does planning by rollouts use an explicit dynamics model?
options: It predicts the next frame's pixels for each action.
It replays recorded trajectories from real hardware.
It trains the model on every action the robot takes.
It simulates candidate actions and picks the best one.
questions.explanation: next_state = f(state, action) lets a planner try options without touching hardware, then act on the best.

questions.prompt: When does an explicit dynamics model stop being practical?
options: When the robot has fewer than six degrees of freedom
When no good state space can be defined by hand
When planning needs more than one step ahead
When the training data includes images
questions.explanation: Hand-defined state works for simple problems. Rich raw sensory input needs learned representations, which is what perception and JEPA provide.

questions.prompt: The collapsed run's loss was 0.000003, far below the healthy run's 0.000833. Which was better?
options: Neither, since both losses are near zero.
They are equal, since loss and spread cancel out.
The collapsed run, since its loss is lower.
The healthy run, with about 14x the spread.
questions.explanation: The collapsed run maps everything to almost one point. A loss curve can't tell the two apart. The variance check can.

questions.prompt: The real predictor's MSE was 0.00080 and the always-predict-the-mean baseline's 0.03201. How many times better is the real predictor? Give a whole number.
questions.explanation: 0.03201 / 0.00080 = 40.0. The book reports 40.1x from unrounded values. The model uses its input, not a dataset average.

questions.prompt: A team's joint-embedding model reaches very low loss very fast. What should they do first?
options: Remove the EMA target, since it slows convergence.
Check embedding variance against a random encoder's.
Lower the learning rate, since the loss fell too quickly.
Celebrate, since low loss means good representations.
questions.explanation: Procedure 60.3 says suspiciously good loss is the first symptom to check. A spread around 10x below a random encoder suggests collapse. Removing the EMA would cause it.

questions.prompt: How does a JEPA differ from a plain autoencoder?
options: Its target is a separately encoded view.
It needs labels, while autoencoders don't.
It reconstructs its input pixel for pixel.
It has no encoder, only a predictor.
questions.explanation: An autoencoder's target is its own input. JEPA's asymmetry between context and target is the point, and removing it caused collapse in the worked example.

bookExercises.prompt: Name the three broad families of world model and state, for each, what it predicts (frame, embedding, or state).
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Pixel-space generative models predict the next frame, pixel by pixel. Latent/representation predictors (JEPA family) predict the next embedding. Explicit dynamics models predict the next state in a hand-defined state space.

bookExercises.prompt: Name JEPA's three architectural components and state which one receives gradients directly during training.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Context encoder, target encoder, predictor. The context encoder is the only one receiving gradients directly during training. The target encoder updates only via EMA, with no gradient of its own, and the predictor is trained via the loss between its output and the target encoder's output.

bookExercises.prompt: Using the Worked Example's healthy-vs-collapsed comparison (loss 0.000833 vs. 0.000003, embedding std 0.00540 vs. 0.00039), explain why a monitoring dashboard tracking only training loss would have flagged the WORSE run as the better one, and what specifically Procedure 60.3's check adds that loss alone doesn't provide.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A dashboard tracking only loss would see the collapsed run's loss (0.000003) as dramatically better than the healthy run's (0.000833) and flag it as the superior model. Loss alone has no way to distinguish "learned to predict accurately" from "learned to output nearly the same value regardless of input," since both produce a very small prediction error once the target itself has collapsed to near-constant. Procedure 60.3's variance check adds exactly the missing information: it measures whether the embeddings themselves carry meaningful spread across different inputs (0.00540 for the healthy run vs. 0.00039 for the collapsed run, roughly 14x smaller). A low loss with a collapsed embedding spread reveals the low loss is cheap and meaningless, not evidence of good prediction.

bookExercises.prompt: Using the Worked Example's mean-baseline comparison (real predictor MSE 0.00080 vs. mean-baseline MSE 0.03201, a 40.1x gap), explain why this specific check is necessary even when Procedure 60.3's variance check already looks healthy. What different failure mode does each check rule out?
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The variance check (Procedure 60.3) catches representation collapse: the model mapping every input to nearly the same embedding, making prediction trivially easy. The mean-baseline check catches a different failure mode: even with genuine, non-collapsed variance in the embeddings, the predictor itself could still be ignoring its context input and just learning to output the batch's average target embedding, which is a different kind of shortcut that a variance check alone wouldn't necessarily catch (the target encoder's embeddings could have healthy spread while the *predictor* still cheats by ignoring context and outputting something close to the mean target). Both checks are necessary because they isolate different components: variance checks the encoder/representations; the mean-baseline check specifically verifies the predictor is actually using its input rather than only the target distribution's central tendency.

bookExercises.prompt: A colleague sees a JEPA-style model's loss drop unusually fast during training and reports "great, the model converged early." Using this chapter's Worked Example, write the two or three sentences you'd say before accepting that as good news.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "Before celebrating, check the embedding variance directly, not just the loss. This chapter's own Worked Example showed a collapsed run's loss dropping to 0.000003, nearly 300x lower than a healthy run's 0.000833, while its embedding spread was about 14x smaller, meaning it had learned to output nearly the same value for every input rather than actually learning to predict. An unusually fast, unusually low loss on a joint-embedding model is specifically the symptom to be suspicious of, not celebrate, until the variance check confirms it isn't collapse."

bookExercises.prompt: Procedure 60.1 warns that masking too little makes the task trivial. Describe concretely what a predictor could learn to do with a 5% mask ratio that it couldn't do with a 50% mask ratio, and why that shortcut wouldn't require learning genuine scene structure.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: With only a 5% mask ratio, nearly all of an image's patches remain visible, so the predictor could learn to simply copy or lightly interpolate from the small number of masked patches' immediate visible neighbours. Spatially adjacent patches in a real image are often nearly identical or smoothly varying, so a near-complete context lets the predictor solve the task through local copying/interpolation rather than genuinely understanding the scene's broader structure. At a 50% mask ratio, entire regions can be hidden with no immediately-adjacent visible patch to copy from, forcing the predictor to actually use higher-level structural understanding (object shape, scene layout) to make a reasonable prediction, since simple local copying is no longer sufficient.

bookExercises.prompt: Read about VICReg's variance-covariance regularisation approach, mentioned in this chapter's Exposition as an alternative to an EMA target encoder. Explain in your own words why VICReg doesn't need a second (target) encoder at all, unlike JEPA and BYOL.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: VICReg doesn't need a second encoder because it prevents collapse through an explicit loss term rather than an architectural asymmetry: it directly penalises any embedding dimension whose variance across the batch falls below a threshold, making the trivial "collapse everything to one point" solution actively costly to the loss function rather than architecturally hard to reach. JEPA and BYOL instead rely on the EMA target encoder's slow, gradient-free updates to prevent the target from collapsing in lockstep with the online network, an architectural mechanism. VICReg substitutes a direct mathematical penalty for that architectural trick, so there's no need for two separately-updated networks at all. A single encoder trained with the variance (and covariance) regularisation term added to its loss is sufficient.
